opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think a few things are pushing in that direction at once.

The first is just the economics. Inference is becoming the dominant workload. Training is a big upfront cost, but once you deploy a model that millions of people use every day, the inference bill keeps growing and eventually dwarfs the training bill. When that much money is at stake, everyone has a strong incentive to look for cheaper ways to serve tokens. Even a 20 or 30 percent improvement in cost per token adds up to an enormous amount of money at that scale.

The second is that inference is a more constrained, better-understood problem than training. With training you need a lot of flexibility: researchers try new architectures, new optimizers, all kinds of weird things, and NVIDIA's software ecosystem, CUDA, all the libraries, the tooling, is a huge advantage there. Inference is much more specialized. You have a fixed model, mostly running matrix multiplies and attention, and the bottlenecks are fairly clear: memory bandwidth, especially during decoding, and moving the KV cache around. When the workload is that well defined, it's much easier for a specialized chip to target it and do well. That's why you see AMD getting more traction, the hyperscalers building their own chips like TPUs, Trainium, and Maia, and startups designing hardware around specific parts of inference.

The third is that the software layer is getting more portable. A few years ago, if you wanted to run on non-NVIDIA hardware, you were basically on your own. Now there are compilers and higher-level kernel languages like Triton, plus inference engines that support multiple backends, so the cost of switching hardware is going down. A lot of my own work has been on writing very low-level kernels, and one thing I've seen is that once you understand the algorithm well, the ideas carry over. You have to rewrite things for each architecture, but the core insights about IO-awareness and memory hierarchy are the same across chips.

And finally, the workloads themselves are diversifying. You have long-context inference, agentic workloads with many steps, reasoning models that generate a lot of tokens, small models running on the edge, and different architectures like state space models or hybrids. Those have pretty different hardware profiles. Some are compute-bound, some are memory-bound, some care about latency, some about throughput. I don't think one chip will be optimal for all of them.

So I don't think NVIDIA is going away. They're still excellent and their software lead is real. But I expect the inference market to look much more heterogeneous, with different chips winning different slices of the workload. That's actually healthy for the field, because competition pushes the cost of intelligence down, and that's what lets these models be used much more widely.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the big picture is that inference is just a very different workload from training, and the hardware that's optimal for one isn't necessarily optimal for the other. For training, you want massive FLOPs, you want everything connected with really high bandwidth interconnects, and NVIDIA has been incredibly good at building that whole stack. But when you look at inference, especially with these large language models, you're often bottlenecked not by compute but by memory bandwidth. You're loading the weights, you're loading the KV cache, and the actual matrix multiplies are relatively small per token, particularly in the decode phase.

So the question becomes: what's the best chip for moving a lot of bytes around cheaply? And that opens the door to a lot of different designs. You have companies like Cerebras and Groq building architectures with huge amounts of on-chip SRAM, so they can get really low latency per token. You have AMD with the MI300 series, which has a lot of HBM capacity, which is great for serving big models. You have the hyperscalers, Google with TPUs, Amazon with Trainium and Inferentia, building their own silicon because at their scale the cost savings are enormous. And then there's a whole wave of startups doing more specialized things.

The other piece is that the workload itself is diversifying. It's not just one big model doing chat anymore. You have long-context workloads where the KV cache dominates. You have agentic workloads with lots of short calls. You have mixture-of-experts models where the memory and routing patterns look different. You have things like test-time compute where you're generating tons of tokens for reasoning. Each of these has a different profile, and that makes it harder for one architecture to be the best at everything.

And honestly, part of why I'm optimistic is that the software layer is maturing. A big reason NVIDIA has had such a lock is CUDA, and the fact that all the kernels, FlashAttention included, were written for it first. But now you have things like Triton, you have better compilers, you have more people writing kernels for AMD and for other targets. As that gap closes, the switching cost goes down, and then the economics of inference, where cost per token really matters, start to push people toward whatever gives them the best price-performance for their specific workload. I don't think NVIDIA goes away, they'll be a huge player, but I expect the landscape to look a lot more heterogeneous in a few years.

astra-6.text:
I think inference is a more natural place for hardware diversity than training. With training, you need a lot of flexibility because you’re changing the model, trying new architectures, debugging things. NVIDIA’s software ecosystem is a huge advantage there.

With inference, once you have a model that you’re going to serve at scale, you can justify spending a lot of engineering effort to make it run efficiently on a particular chip. And different workloads want different things. Processing a long prompt looks very different from generating one token at a time. Some applications care most about latency; others care about throughput or power consumption.

So there’s room for different hardware to do well on different parts of that space. The challenge is software: can you actually get the model running reliably and realize the hardware’s theoretical advantage? NVIDIA is very strong there. But as inference becomes a bigger expense, the incentive to build those alternatives gets much stronger.

sol-6.1.text:
I think inference is going to be a much more diverse market because the workloads themselves are so diverse. Training a large model tends to involve a fairly similar set of operations, and you care a lot about how quickly you can finish a big run. With inference, you might care about latency for one user, throughput across thousands of users, power consumption, or running on a device. Those constraints lead to different hardware choices.

Even within language models, processing the prompt and generating tokens have different bottlenecks. Prompt processing can be very compute intensive, while token generation is often limited by moving model weights and the KV cache around. So there’s room for hardware optimized for different parts of that workload.

NVIDIA has a very strong software ecosystem, and that’s a huge advantage. But if you’re serving the same model millions of times, it can be worth investing in the software to make another chip work well, especially if the economics are better. I’d expect multiple kinds of hardware to coexist.
